Modern.brandNameRationale: Bedside is the medical-trade term for caring presence with a patient. Telehealth is the plain category suffix. Stands in the lineage of trade-vocabulary modern telehealth brands.
Modern.industrySummary: Telehealth has moved from emergency-pandemic option to default for primary care, mental health, and chronic management. The customer is design-literate and demanding. Modern entrants are competing on app quality, clinical depth, and brand clarity.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Hims & Hers (forhims.com / forhers.com) holds the modern D2C telehealth peer. Ro (ro.co) sits in the same tier. Plushcare (plushcare.com) does the primary-care-led version. Galileo (galileo.io) holds the design-led middle. We sit closest to Galileo in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: Primary care delivered remotely, with the same standards as the clinic.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two words. Concord suggests an established place name or principle of agreement. Medical names the category clinically. The pair reads like an old medical institution that quietly added a modern telehealth practice. Trusted, considered, and not at all startup.
Luxury.story: Concord Medical began as an in-person practice. The current principals added a small telehealth arm to serve clients who travel, who hold homes in multiple cities, or who simply prefer the convenience. The telehealth practice accepts a limited number of patients each year.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end telehealth has been dominated by scaling consumer services. There's a parallel market for small concierge telehealth practices in the older tradition. Few patients, long relationships, doctor on call. The customer is paying for the physician, the access, and the discretion.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Sollis Health (sollishealth.com) holds the concierge-medicine telehealth tier. Forward (goforward.com), before its troubles, was the technology-led peer. Eight Sleep Health, and similar small concierge clinics, are the closest. We sit smaller and more heritage in tone.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small concierge practice with telehealth as part of the relationship.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy. Often inherited. Travels. Has multiple homes. Values discretion and continuity of care with a single physician across geography and time.

dos: Speak in the language of medicine, not wellness

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn caduceus reduced to two crossed lines, used as a hallmark on letterhead, the brass plaque outside the practice, and the printed visit summaries.

colorPalette.meaning: Old leather, library walls, the waiting room.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Ask is what the patient is doing. The brand sits on the smallest unit of the telehealth offer: ask a doctor, get a response. Plain. Direct. Useful.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most telehealth brands compete on tier and convenience. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the basic act: ask a doctor a question, get a real answer.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most telehealth apps have grown into platforms with multiple services. We compete on the smallest possible scope: question in, answer out. The closest peer in spirit is K Health (khealth.com) but with a sharper minimal interface.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Ask a doctor a question. Get a real answer in writing.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who have a single medical question and don't want to schedule a visit. They want the answer, the next step, and a clear price.

dos: Show the question, the doctor, the answer

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. ASK in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps, three letters with generous space. No icon. The app icon is the wordmark on a soft grey background.

typography.rationale: One face. The app is the wordmark, the question, the answer. Nothing else.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Pioneer signals scale and first-mover credibility. Telehealth Group names the holding-company category. The whole name reads like a real, established telehealth-services firm already on the procurement panel at major health plans and self-insured employers.
Corporate.industrySummary: Enterprise telehealth infrastructure (platform, clinical network, reporting) is a serious B2B category. Health plans, self-insured employers, and integrated health systems need partners who can deliver telehealth at scale with regulatory-grade reporting.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Teladoc (teladoc.com) is the giant. Amwell (amwell.com) holds the institutional peer position. Doctor on Demand, now part of Included Health (includedhealth.com), sits in the same tier. We sit smaller and more focused on the contemporary enterprise integration side.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Telehealth infrastructure for health plans and self-insured employers.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Health plans and large employers need telehealth partners with clinical depth and integration discipline. The category incumbents are big and slow. We sit between them, with the operating model the modern enterprise buyer needs.

targetAudience.primary: Chief Medical Officers, VPs of Benefits, and Population Health Directors at self-insured employers, health plans, and integrated health systems. They sign multi-year contracts.

Creative.tagline: A telehealth brand built around the call.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Clinic Line is the trade phrase for the medical phone line — the call that connects the patient to the practice. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade-name school.
Creative.manifesto: Most telehealth brands sound like a health insurance company trying to be your friend. They overpromise, underexplain, and outsource the warmth. We made Hey Doc for the moment a person actually asks for medical help: tired, uncertain, just wanting to talk to a doctor without a form. The brand is the casual front door of medicine.
Creative.industrySummary: Telehealth branding has been polished, professional, and slightly cold. There's room for a brand that's warm, character-driven, sticker-friendly, and still serious about clinical depth.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Hims & Hers (forhims.com) does the casual-direct middle. Galileo (galileo.io) sits in the design-led peer group. Cleo (hicleo.com) holds the parenting-care side. We sit warmer than all of them, with a clearer voice.
Creative.positioningStatement: A telehealth brand that sounds like a real friend, not an insurance company.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 45. Has insurance, doesn't trust it. Already pays out of pocket for some health services. Wants telehealth that feels like talking to a friend who happens to be a doctor.

dos: Talk like the doctor you already know
Make warm jokes about the system
Tell the truth about what telehealth can and can't do
